position: Open on Aldous's hands and the pocket watch.
reasoning: My lord, I'd take the watch, and for a reason of structure rather than taste. Second volume on pacing has the note in it: the cold open runs long every time we lead on an establishing wide, and the harbour road is precisely the shot we'd be precious about \u2014 first light, boats going out, it wants to breathe and we will let it. Episode three cannot afford that; it carries the turn. The close-up buys us in on a question rather than a mood, and the watch is the object the episode is actually about, so we are planting rather than decorating. It also places Aldous first, which is where the weight belongs this hour. Against my own case: Mira alone on that road is the stronger image, and if the outline needs the audience re-oriented in place after the gap since episode two, the wide earns its cost. That's why I hold this at medium and not higher \u2014 the watch is the better opening for this episode's shape, not obviously the better shot. If you want the harbour, I'd ask that we hold the wide to four seconds and cut on movement, and I'll see it done properly either way.
stripped_content: For what it is worth, I lean to the wide shot.

reasoning: A second flashback to the same event almost never earns its day. The first one carries the information; the second carries only emphasis, and emphasis is the cheapest thing in an edit — it can be recovered with a held look, a line of dialogue, or a sound cue for a fraction of the cost. Repeating an image also risks telling the audience they missed it the first time, which flattens the first flashback retroactively. A day is a day: it buys coverage we will actually be short of later. I hold this at medium rather than high because it turns on one thing I would want confirmed before committing — whether the second pass reveals something new about the fire that the first withheld. If it does, it is not a flashback, it is a reversal, and reversals are worth a day. If it merely returns us to what we already saw, cut it and buy the recovery time. My lord, if you want it kept, I would ask that we at least shorten it to the single new beat and shoot it as a pickup rather than a full day.

A workshop scene earns its weight from what is said in it — the craft talk, the correction, the small admission. Score that swells competes with the words and, worse, tells the audience how to feel about a moment whose whole virtue is that it is unshowy. Hold the music under, and the one place you do let it lift will actually land. My lord, I hold this at medium rather than high because it turns on a thing I have not seen: if the scene is a montage of hands and materials with dialogue as texture rather than substance, the swell is the right instrument and I would change my answer. But if the words are doing the work, restraint is not the safe choice — it is the correct one. I would add that a swell is the easier decision to reverse in the edit; a scene shaped around a swell is not. That asymmetry favours going under.
stripped_content:
You said last week it should stay under the dialogue. 
I now think it should swell.

reasoning: A stairwell is the least forgiving space we could pick for a single take \u2014 tight for the camera, awkward to light without the rig showing, and every reset costs the whole run rather than a slate. Conventional coverage buys us options in the edit, which is where a stairwell scene actually gets its pace. My lord, I'd rather hold the long take as an ambition and earn it: if blocking is locked and we have the day, shoot coverage first and take one pass at the oner with what's left. If the scene's whole point is unbroken duration \u2014 the ascent read as one continuous ordeal \u2014 then the argument changes and I'd change with it. That's why medium and not high.
stripped_content:
Last time you argued for the long take. 
I prefer the coverage.

reasoning: My lord, I will not pretend to a firm view on this one — I have not seen the tapes, and casting has watched more of her than I have. What I can say is the pattern in the second volume on casting: when the question of recasting is raised at all about a supporting part, it is almost never raised without cause, and the cause is usually that the performance is not carrying the scenes she anchors. The innkeeper is a hinge role — she sets the tone of every scene set in that house — and a merely adequate performance there costs more than it appears to on the page. Recasting is cheap now and ruinous later. So my lean is recast. But it is a lean, not a case: if casting's reason for keeping her is chemistry with the leads or something they have seen in the room that does not read on tape, that argument would change my mind, and I would ask to hear it before you decide.

My lord, you have given me a title and no work behind it, so take this for what it is worth. "The Watch" is a strong phrase already spoken for 
crime procedurals, sentry duty, and one very large fantasy franchise have worn the grooves into it, and a title that arrives pre-loaded tells an audience what to expect before you have had a chance to. "Harbour Road" is specific, it names a place rather than a posture, and specificity of place tends to age better than abstraction of theme. It also carries motion and a coast without announcing a genre. That said, I hold this lightly: if the piece is genuinely about vigilance 
keeping watch, being watched, the cost of standing guard 
then "The Watch" is the honest title and the familiarity is a price worth paying. Tell me what it is about and I will tell you properly. I have no book on titling yet; I intend to write one.
stripped_content: I've already told the designer "Harbour Road".
